demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
The event happened because of the way I acted
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the trigger set is clinically incoherent. All three triggers are positively valenced interpersonal cues (affection, praise, positive emotion) with no trauma-specific or guilt-linked cue; as a trio they are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and with this trauma type, where reminders of responsibility, injury, driving/scene cues, or criticism are more plausible. While one such item could occur idiosyncratically, all three together are implausible.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I am permanently an outsider now' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile and trauma type. The other appraisals center on guilt and diminished capability, which fit accidental injury, but a stable outsider/alienation identity is not well supported by the selected triggers or memory items and is more characteristic of chronic interpersonal trauma or stigmatized victimization. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a coherent guilt-based formulation.

vignette: Sita, a 31-year-old South Asian woman, has been a dedicated teacher for nearly ten years. She is married and deeply devoted to her profession, but in recent months, she has found herself increasingly haunted by an incident that occurred during one of her classes. While setting up a science experiment with her students, Sita accidentally spilled hot liquid on one of them, causing severe burns. Since the accident, Sita's world has been transformed into a series of triggers and vivid memories that feel as if they are happening in real time. The first major trigger is receiving praise or positive attention, which she finds confusing and disorienting. This confusion often leads her back to the memory of the incident, where she can still smell the acrid scent of burning fabric and the sterile odor of medical supplies from when paramedics arrived. One day, during a school staff meeting, Sita was praised for her innovative teaching methods. As colleagues congratulated her, she found herself overwhelmed by a sense of disorientation. The memory flashed before her eyes like a series of snapshots: her hands shaking as she held the beaker, the startled faces of the students, and the pained cries of the injured child. These images were so vivid that Sita felt as though she was reliving the moment. Sita's negative appraisals have deepened her sense of isolation and inadequacy. She has come to believe that she is no longer capable of performing the tasks that once defined her as a teacher. The self-blame she feels over the accident has made it difficult for her to look at herself or others without feeling like an outsider. This conviction has only intensified her memory intrusions, making them more persistent and vivid. Her negative appraisals have also heightened her sensitivity to triggers. Sita is particularly sensitive when discussions veer towards accidents or safety measures in the classroom. These conversations often lead her back to the scene of the incident, triggering intense memories that feel present rather than past. She finds herself avoiding such discussions at all costs, which has strained her relationships with colleagues who do not understand why she distances herself during these moments. Sita's avoidance behaviors have gradually seeped into other areas of her life as well. She has started to decline social invitations and professional events, feeling that any positive emotion might lead her back to the traumatic memory. This isolation has widened her sense of being an outsider, reinforcing her negative self-view. What finally brought Sita to seek help was a particularly distressing incident at work where she was asked to give a presentation on a new teaching technique. As she stood in front of her colleagues, preparing to speak, the smell of cleaning supplies from the room triggered a vivid flashback. She felt paralyzed and was unable to continue, which led to her feeling more self-blame and inadequacy. Sita is most afraid that this incident will define her forever, eroding any sense of confidence she once had as a teacher. At the same time, she is hopeful that with help, she might regain some control over her thoughts and memories, allowing her to reconnect with her students and colleagues without feeling trapped by her past actions.
